title: Time Series Clustering for Customer Behavior Segmentation: A Genetic Algorithm Approach
venue: Journal of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence
tldr: Combining a genetic algorithm with k-means clustering achieves optimal customer segmentation based on RFM (recency, frequency, monetary) transaction patterns, outperforming traditional k-means alone.
problem_and_motivation: Customer behavior segmentation is essential for targeted marketing, but traditional clustering methods like k-means are sensitive to initial centroid selection and local optima. Time series transaction data with RFM dimensions requires more robust clustering approaches to capture temporal spending patterns.
approach: Used transaction dataset from an Iranian payment company containing 12,000 customer records with transaction timestamps, amounts, and merchant categories.
Extracted RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) features along with payment cost and average transaction amount per customer.
Applied a two-phase approach: genetic algorithm optimization followed by k-means clustering.
Genetic algorithm evolved initial centroids over 100 generations with population size 50, crossover rate 0.8, and mutation rate 0.1.
Compared GA-optimized k-means against standard k-means and k-means++ using Silhouette Score and Davies-Bouldin Index.
Evaluated clustering stability across different numbers of clusters (k = 3 to 8).
findings: GA-optimized k-means achieves Silhouette Score of 0.72 vs. 0.58 for standard k-means and 0.64 for k-means++.
Davies-Bouldin Index improves from 1.34 (standard k-means) to 0.89 (GA-optimized), indicating better cluster separation.
Four distinct customer segments emerged: high-frequency high-value (12%), moderate-frequency regular (35%), low-frequency occasional (41%), and dormant (12%).
GA optimization converges after approximately 60 generations, with Silhouette Score stabilizing at 0.71–0.72.
The high-frequency segment (12%) generates 38% of total revenue, confirming Pareto principle in customer spending.
Dormant customers (12%) have average recency of 180 days vs. 15 days for high-frequency segment.
Feature scaling significantly affects clustering quality: Min-Max normalization outperforms Z-score for RFM data.
Computational cost of GA optimization is 3.2x higher than standard k-means but justified by 24% improvement in Silhouette Score.

key_equations.explanation: Silhouette Score measuring cluster quality, where a(i) is average intra-cluster distance and b(i) is minimum average inter-cluster distance.
Davies-Bouldin Index measuring average similarity ratio of each cluster to its most similar cluster, where lower values indicate better clustering.
Feature vector representing customer transaction behavior through time since last purchase, number of transactions, and total spending.

definitions.definition: Customer segmentation method using Recency (time since last purchase), Frequency (number of transactions), and Monetary value (total spending) to classify customers.
Optimization heuristic inspired by natural selection that evolves candidate solutions through selection, crossover, and mutation over generations.
Clustering evaluation metric measuring how similar an object is to its own cluster compared to other clusters, ranging from -1 to 1.
Clustering evaluation metric measuring average similarity ratio of each cluster to its most similar cluster, where lower values indicate better separation.
Partitioning algorithm that groups data into k clusters by minimizing within-cluster sum of squared distances from centroids.
Improved k-means initialization method that selects initial centroids to be as far apart as possible.

topics.name: Clustering and Segmentation Algorithms for Transaction Data
topics.justification: Directly applies clustering algorithms (k-means, GA-optimized k-means) to segment customers based on RFM transaction patterns, demonstrating advanced segmentation methodology.

topics.name: Real-Time Anomaly Detection and Spending Pattern Alerts
topics.justification: The GA-optimized clustering approach for transaction data is applicable to detecting anomalous spending patterns by identifying deviations from established customer segments.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper demonstrates that genetic algorithm optimization significantly improves k-means clustering for customer segmentation based on RFM transaction data. It identifies four distinct customer segments with clear behavioral profiles and shows that the GA-optimized approach achieves 24% better Silhouette Score than standard k-means. The methodology is directly applicable to financial data clustering and spending pattern analysis.
directly_justifies: GA-optimized k-means achieves 0.72 Silhouette Score vs. 0.58 for standard k-means.
Four customer segments emerge with clear RFM profiles: high-frequency (12%), moderate (35%), low-frequency (41%), dormant (12%).
The high-frequency segment generates 38% of total revenue, confirming Pareto principle.
GA optimization converges after ~60 generations with computational cost 3.2x standard k-means.
Min-Max normalization outperforms Z-score for RFM transaction data clustering.
limits: Dataset limited to Iranian payment company transactions, which may not generalize to other markets.
RFM features do not capture qualitative aspects of customer behavior or merchant preferences.
Computational cost of GA optimization (3.2x) may be prohibitive for very large datasets.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: A systematic scan of all topic domains was conducted. Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) was selected because the paper directly applies clustering algorithms to transaction data for customer segmentation. Domain 5 (Anomaly Detection & Early-Warning Systems) was flagged because the clustering methodology is applicable to detecting anomalous spending patterns by identifying deviations from established segments.

limitations: Iranian payment company dataset may not represent spending patterns in other economies.
RFM features exclude qualitative merchant and product preference information.
GA optimization adds 3.2x computational cost, which may be prohibitive for very large datasets.
